problem.text: Which expression is equal to $\left|\,a-2-\sqrt{(a-1)^2}\,\right|$ for $a<0$?

steps.title: Where to start: a square root of a square
steps.body: The clue is $\sqrt{(a-1)^2}$. Squaring throws away the sign, and the square root always gives back a number that is at least $0$. So the square root of a square is an absolute value: $$\sqrt{t^2} = |t|.$$

steps.title: Remove the inner absolute value
steps.body: So $\sqrt{(a-1)^2} = |a-1|$. Since $a<0$, the number $a-1$ is negative, so $|a-1| = 1-a$. Careful: writing $\sqrt{(a-1)^2} = a-1$ is the most common mistake here, and it is wrong whenever $a-1<0$.

your_turn.prompt: Check with $a=-2$: what is $\sqrt{(a-1)^2}$, and does it match $1-a$?

steps.title: Simplify the inside
steps.body: Now replace the square root by $1-a$, so the expression inside the outer bars is $a-2-(1-a)$. Careful with the minus sign in front of the parentheses: it changes the sign of both terms inside.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: When $a<0$, the number $2a-3$ is negative, so its absolute value is its opposite: $$|2a-3| = 3-2a.$$ Check with $a=-1$: the original expression is $|-1-2-2| = 5$, and $3-2(-1) = 5$. The answer is **(A)** $3-2a$.

wrong_choices.C: This comes from replacing $\sqrt{(a-1)^2}$ by $a-1$: then the inside is $a-2-(a-1) = -1$ and you get $1$. But $a-1$ is negative here, so the square root must be $1-a$.
wrong_choices.E: This comes from a sign slip: writing $a-2-(1-a)$ as $a-2-1-a = -3$. The minus sign must flip both terms, so $-(1-a) = -1+a$.

verification.verifier_notes: Passed adversarial verifier on first review.
